items.title: 68356_Howard R. Scott oral history interview
items.q: And what few there were lived downtown, and gradually, around 1910, Coleman Johnson was a team in vaudeville.

ctx.x: I says, hey, wait a minute, fellows. Come on, we're going to get a little bite in here. I said, that's Lindy's, isn't it? Gee, that's a ________ place, all the show people went in there. Of course, we all had tuxedos on. We lived in tuxedos all the time. You're with us, Scottie, come on. (Inaudible) never mind, we can go down the street there at the

automat and get something. No, no, come on in. Well, the four of us went in, we sat at a table, and I was served. And that's the way it's been with me most of my life. Now, I didn't come in contact with any discrimination that they talk about and all like that. I didn't experience any of it, because when I was born in New York, -- we all lived downtown. When I was born, there was no colored people in Harlem at all. None at all. And what few there were lived downtown, and gradually, around 1910, Coleman Johnson…

Well, they were decent respectable people that moved in there. And gradually, a house opened here and there and there, and finally, we came to Harlem. And when we got there, everybody on the block knew everybody else, white or colored. Because across the street from us was all white. It was four colored people on our block, four houses, I mean. We visited each other, yeah. The women knew each other, visiting and all like that.
